description.narrative: Reporting is an important management tool which is used to inform relevant government officials and other stakeholders about the results being achieved by individual projects and the programme as a whole. For project partners, it is compulsory to use the prescribed Orange Knowledge annual report format in order to report on project achievements. The annual report also provides valuable data on the financial situation of the project. Based on an analysis of the project performance in relation to the project output(s) and expected outcome(s), a revision of the project work plan may be suggested by the project partners. The consequences of a possible revision on the project work plan and budget must be made clear in the annual report. Nuffic monitors outputs and outcomes and not activities . Therefore, the main focus of the annual report must be on the achievement of the project’s output(s) and planned outcome(s). The information provided in the annual reports of the projects is used by Nuffic to monitor the progress of the project and to inform the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and other stakeholders about the output(s) and outcome(s) being achieved by individual projects and the Orange Knowledge programme as a whole. Please note that if project progress is in accordance with the original planning, reporting requirements are minimal. Only in case of deviations from the planning, more elaboration is demanded. In the grant award letter, the dates for submission of the annual reports are mentioned. In case of a three-year project, between 5-7 reports are obligatory. The first report (0) is a very short report which focuses on specific conditions and/or recommendations in the grant. There is no need to report on progress in achieving outputs and outcomes, which is done in the first annual report. As annex to the report 0, the consortium agreements between the partners should be submitted. The final report must reflect on the entire project period.

actual.value:
++**Output 1 - First milestone - Project launch meeting (completely achieved)**++
A first meeting with the National TVET Ad Hoc Coordination Committee (requesting partner) was held on 31st of March 2022. The launching then took place on Monday 25th April 2022 at the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs Conference Hall. A total of 92 participants comprising of 42 females and 50 males participated. These were representatives from the key Government Ministries whose mandate are linked to the project. These participants included those from the National Ministry of General Education and Instruction, Ministry of Youth and Sports, Ministry of Gender, Child and Social welfare, Ministry of Agriculture and Food security, Ministry of Animal Resources and Fisheries. Also in attendance were the representatives of the Pastoral communities, Women in milk trading business and NGO that work with the pastoral communities. The launch began by a 20 minutes’ video recording presented to the participants on the way of life in the cattle camps. This was followed by a powerpoint presentation of the project by the local consultant. Upon the presentation of the project, the floor was opened for questions and answers and points of clarification. Over 30 participants requested for the chance to talk and they all appreciated the choice of the project and the target beneficiaries. The main challenge was on the little project funding and how to scale-up the project to reach to all the pastoral communities across South Sudan. South Sudan is divided into 13 subnational Government and it is only Western Equatoria and Western Bar El Gazal states that are not having the pastoral communities.
++**Output 2 - Second milestone - Training needs assessment (completely achieved)**++
A training needs assessment was conducted for the artisanal milk production sector across South Sudan. A total of 97 respondents were contacted across the 13 subnational governments. The respondents included the community livestock extension workers across the 13 Directorates of Livestock and Animal Resources, the Livestock skills training officers at Marial-Lou livestock training institute, the cattle camp milk producers, the milk sellers and National NGO in the agropastoral livelihood skills. Through a combined approach that included interviews, questionnaires and focus groups discussions, this assessment identified categories of training needs areas in the milk handling, production and processing amongst the youth, women, mobile TVET instructors and livestock extension workers across South Sudan to be covered during the provision of the training. The questionnaire was translated in 7 local languages and administered to the local community who could not properly understand the English language. The results obtained were translated into English language and analysed and then reported. Quantitative and qualitative data were used to assess the training gaps and used to design the training of trainer’s manual.
++**Output 3 - Third milestone - TVET trainer’s manual development (completely achieved)**++
A 5-day workshop was organized in Nakuru, Kenya, in October 2022. iCRA, together with the three Kenyan trainers, the local consultant and two South Sudanese officials (among which the representative of the requesting organization) worked on hands-on training materials (in English). With the needs assessment amongst actors in the artisanal milk supply chain across South Sudan done in August 2022 by the local consultant, we had a clearer view on where to put focus on in the training that will be offered to Trainers in South Sudan in December 2022: introduction, dairy commodities, clean milk production, quality assessment of raw milk, hygiene, ruminant health and nutrition, pedagogical skills, milk business. Overall, at the end of the 5-day workshop, despite some obstacles (see sections 1 and 3), most of the training material had been produced and it had been finalized and printed early December 2022 before the training in Juba.
++**Output 4 - Fourth milestone - TMT (completely achieved)**++
Overall, the TMT, organized from 5th to 10th December 2022 in Juba, South Sudan, went well. The three Kenyan trainers of the project said it was wonderful to visit the cattle camp with 5,000 cattle! We had a good number of very receptive participants and they would want this training to be expanded to other regions of South Sudan. Most participants work for local NGO (Women Advancement Organization, Women Union, Women in Small business, Aid Support Community Organization, …) and some of them (15 women) already started doing milk business following the training, and started to train other. There is clearly a need and willingness from the team to continue to support the participants after the project ends. Participants from Marial-Lou Livestock Training Institute (government entity, 3h flight from Juba) will develop their own curricula based on our manual.
++Topics of the training that were actually delivered by the three Kenyan trainers (Jerono KIPTANUI, Menach EVANS and Kisilu KITAINGE)++: pedagogical and soft skills, basic numeracy, basic business approaches, cow nutrition, clean milk production, hygiene and safety, simple ways of testing of milk quality, business opportunity along the milk value chain, hygienic milk production, hygienic post-harvest milk handling and transportation, milk quality testing, grading and rejection (organoleptic, lactometer and clot-on-boiling tests), milk pasteurisation, packaging and storage (by direct and indirect heating), starter culture handling and activation, aseptic propagation and maintenance of starter culture, production of a mesophilic culture fermented milk product (mala), production of a thermophilic culture fermented milk product (yoghurt), cream separation and pasteurisation, ghee making, packaging and storage, butter making, cheese making.
++Extent to which these topics answered the needs of the participants++: participants sorely lacked these skills, the topics were all relevant since the training objectives were to train master trainers in order to pass on the skills to more stakeholders in the milk value chain and they appreciated it and said more time was required to adequately cover the topics.
++What were the participants able to do BEFORE and AFTER the training?++ Most milk products in Juba are imported. BEFORE the training, most participants were familiar with the traditional way of milking, boiling milk, handling and processing of milk. They could milk cows and sell the milk raw or let it ferment spontaneously. Hygiene level was very low. They did not even care to filter/strain the milk. AFTER the training, they were able to appreciate the importance of clean milk production for the overall production of milk products. They were able to correctly boil/pasteurized milk by direct and indirect heating, make mala from commercial culture and from previous mala and yoghurt of various flavours, and actually drunk it and took some home. They were aware of the importance of sieving milk (we demonstrated sieving in the cattle camp and there were hairs, dust, ticks, dung, etc.). We demonstrated how to milk correctly by full hand rather than stripping. They were able to test quality of milk such as organoleptic, use of lactometer, etc. They were able to detect mastitis by use of a strip cup or any black container. They were able to know how to make feed ration for a dairy cow. They learned on milk borne diseases such as brucellosis and tuberculosis and how to prevent it by proper boiling. They learned some common animal disease that has direct or indirect effect on milk production or quality.

comment.narrative: 19-09-2023: The number of participants slightly differ for each training day (6-7-8-9 December 2022). However, there were 13 South Sudanese TVET trainers (8 men and 5 women) who attended every training day. They were joined by milk producers (mostly women), milk processors (mostly women) and milk sellers (mostly women) and governmental representatives (mostly men). The high number of women is justified by the fact that dairy activities in South Sudan are mostly a women affair. Moreover, among those women were "returnees" (from diverse profiles), but it was difficult to clearly identified the specific context.
